Shri Sourabh Agarwal - Advocate for respondent.

Order 
The present application under Section 378(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code for leave to appeal has been filed by the State against the order dated 30.12.2014 passed in Case No. 2294/2011, whereby the respondent was acquitted of the charges under Sections 7(1) read with 16(1) (A)(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

The prosecution's case, in brief, is that on 07.05.2011, at approximately 2:15 PM, Food Inspector Naveen Jain conducted an inspection of the accused's ice-cream factory and requested the license for selling food from the accused, who produced receipt No. 007, Book No. 11, dated 14.04.2011,
issued by the Municipal Council.
With the vendor's consent, the inspection was carried out in the presence of witnesses.

During the inspection, the vendor was found to be manufacturing, storing,
and selling various types of ice-cream for human consumption.

With the vendor's consent, a sample of the ice-cream was taken for standard quality NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:31720 2 MCRC-3051-2015 testing, with the total cost of Rs. 72/- paid in cash to the vendor and a receipt obtained.
The ice-cream mixture was thoroughly homogenized, divided into three equal parts, and properly packed, with a panchnama drawn up.

According to the examination report of the ice-cream sample submitted by the Deputy Director, Food and Drug Administration, District Guna, under letter dated 13.07.2011, the sample was found to be adulterated.
Following this, after obtaining proper sanction for prosecution, a complaint was filed against the accused in the court of law.

sentences.text: However, the learned subordinate court, after a careful evaluation of the evidence, rendered a judgment of acquittal.
Learned counsel for the State submitted that the accused had already received the notice under Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

It was contended that although the original receipt of the postal dispatch sent to the accused from the post office was not exhibited in the case record, the accused did not raise any objection during the proceedings claiming that they were denied an opportunity to have the sample tested at another branch of the Central Laboratory.

It was further submitted that the Food Inspector, Naveen Jain, had fully corroborated the prosecution case and occurrence, and that witness Jitendra Saxena had also verified the compliance with the requirements of Section 13(2).
Learned counsel emphasized that there was no material contradiction in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses, which could negate the charges established against the accused.

In view of the foregoing, it was submitted that the order of acquittal passed by the learned trial court is liable to be set aside, as it is NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:31720 3 MCRC-3051-2015 contrary to law and inconsistent with the facts and evidence on record.
Learned counsel for the respondent contended that the trial court, after a careful and thorough examination of the evidence on record, rightly acquitted the respondent of the alleged offences.
The acquittal was based on a proper and comprehensive evaluation of the evidence and is fully in accordance with law.

Any attempt by the State to challenge the acquittal is therefore misconceived,
as the impugned order is neither contrary to law nor inconsistent with the facts of the case.
Heard counsel for the parties and perused the record.

The learned trial court, in the impugned order, acquitted the respondent by holding that in the present case, no letter had been attached to demonstrate that in the event of adulteration in the report of the analysis of samples sent to the Public Analyst under sub-section (1) of Section 13(2) of the Act, the competent authority of the local health office, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, had sent such a notice to the accused along with a copy of the analysis report.
Such notice would have provided the accused an opportunity, within ten days from the date of the decision, to apply to the court for having the food samples analyzed by a Central Laboratory.
In the present case, the local health authority did not comply with Section 13(2) of the Act, and no copy of the notice was attached in the case record.
During cross-examination, Jitendra Saxena stated that the letter sent through Exhibit P.17 was dispatched by ordinary post and not with acknowledgment.

During arguments, the accused cited the judgment of the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:31720 4 MCRC-3051-2015 Coordinate Bench in Ramesh Agrawal v. State of M.P., 2014 F.A.J. 47, wherein it was held that merely dispatching the report to the accused is not sufficient.

entities.text: Ramesh Agrawal v. State of M.P., 2014 F.A.J. 47
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The prosecution must prove that the report was received by the accused in a timely manner, enabling them to have the samples tested in a Central Food Laboratory.
Merely dispatching the notice is, therefore, inadequate.
In the present case, there is no evidence on record to show that the accused had been informed, which is a mandatory requirement.

sentences.text: Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act mandates that the person from whom the sample is taken should be given an opportunity to have the sample tested at a Central Food Laboratory within ten days of receiving the public analyst's report.

In the present case, although the accused did not expressly claim denial of this right during trial, the prosecution has not produced clear evidence to demonstrate strict compliance with this statutory provision.
Non -compliance with Section 13(2) constitutes a procedural irregularity which could vitiate the prosecution case.

In the absence of clear proof that the accused knowingly waived the right to have the sample tested at a Central Laboratory, the procedural safeguard under Section 13(2) cannot be considered fully complied with.
Therefore, the acquittal, on account of non-compliance with a mandatory statutory provision, cannot be interfered with.
In the present case, the learned trial Court has assigned cogent and plausible reasons for acquitting the respondent.
There is no perversity or illegality in the impugned judgment which may warrant interference by this Court at the stage of grant of leave to appeal.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:31720 5 MCRC-3051-2015
Accordingly, this Court finds no merit in the petition.
The petition seeking leave to appeal stands dismissed.
(MILIND RAMESH PHADKE) JUDGE ojha
